title: Everything Done to Prevent It
aliases: What the Ground Will Not Confirm
logline: A ruined twelfth-century citadel on hot, flat inland country, where a ring of brick and clay ninety metres across sits in a grove behind a working village temple, carrying a name, a famous story and a board that explains it, and where the only things anyone has actually dug up are seventeen centuries younger than the story.
human_question: When I am standing in front of something and honestly cannot say what it is, is that the failure — or is the failure the appetite for an answer where nothing can be checked?

place.what_kind_of_place: A ruined royal citadel on low, hot, flat inland country at the island's dry-to-intermediate margin, spread over about twenty hectares and held as an archaeological reserve with a ticket booth and a departmental museum on the road. The citadel proper is rectilinear and diagrammatic: a square brick rampart, a broad moat channel, an east gateway of two brick platforms, and inside it the floor plan of a palace laid out around an open court. About a hundred metres from a working village temple, on the other side of the same reserve, there is a completely different kind of thing — a separate circular earthwork, a ring of brick and clay roughly ninety metres across and some seven metres thick at the base, with concentric clay rings inside it and a small square-chambered foundation at the dead centre. Nothing else like it is known on the island. The ring is what the place is famous for and it is the one structure here that nobody can explain.
place.why_it_is_worth_watching: Three things, and none of them is golden hour. First the geometry: dead flat ground, a straight brick line, a rectangular water channel, and then, four hundred metres away, a perfect circle — plan-drawing shapes at field scale, with no landscape competing for attention. Second the light: old brick under vertical sun goes to two flat tones with no modelling at all, heat comes off it in a visible column, and by the middle of the day the far side of the ring wavers, dissolves and reassembles while the camera holds still. Third, and this is the film, the ring is too big to see from inside it. At eye level it is a horizontal line running out of both edges of the frame. It becomes a circle only from the air, or by walking it until the same broken corner comes back.
place.what_moves_or_changes: Nothing built moves, and that is the point of the treatment. What changes is heat and the eye. Shimmer builds off the brick through the morning and is strongest in the hours a crew would normally avoid. The rampart's shadow shortens to nothing at noon and comes back on the other side. A monitor lizard crosses the moat channel; peafowl walk the palace floor; leaf litter moves in the grove. Visitors arrive at the board, read it, look at the ring and walk on. And the walk itself changes something the camera cannot show: a circuit that leaves every frame identical while the body knows it has gone the whole way round.
place.when_it_looks_best: The driest and hardest part of the year on this ground, roughly late January to March, before the inter-monsoon storms and before April's heat makes long walking work unsafe. The film's core hours are the ones most crews throw away: nine in the morning to about three, with the sun near vertical, the brick bleached and the shimmer at maximum. There is deliberately no dawn and no dusk material. If the aerial is permitted it wants the same flat midday light, because a low sun would model the ring into something prettier and less legible.

two_layers.without_the_philosophy: A hot, still, severely geometric ruin film with a real build and a real payoff and no commentary needed. It opens on a wall that will not resolve into anything. It walks that wall all the way round at eye level and arrives back where it started having learnt nothing. It cuts to the flat horizontal bands of a rampart and a moat at noon. It goes close enough to see salt bloom in a brick joint. Then one continuous vertical climb in which the wall closes into a circle and the whole plan of the place appears at once — and then the same move in reverse, back down to eye level, where it is a wall again. Almost no camera movement except that one rise and fall. No people held in frame. No music cue needed for the turn, because the turn is a shape.
two_layers.with_the_philosophy: The same footage becomes an argument about two kinds of not-knowing standing on the same ground about a thousand years apart. The old one is a statement about the future that people were certain enough about to spend years of labour on. The new one is a visitor in front of a brick circle that may not be the thing the board says it is, on a site whose own name claims a capital the excavations do not support. The voice then does the thing the digests actually license, which is to refuse the obvious verdict in both directions: the commentary is explicit that honest uncertainty about a matter you do not know and cannot properly examine is not the doubt on the list of faults, and the compendium gives that state its own name and says it may not be unwholesome at all. What the sources do warn about is narrower and is the other half of this place: the appetite for a verdict where nothing can be examined. The film never says the prediction was false, never says anything had to happen, and ends on the one honest state available — you can measure this thing exactly and still not know what it is, and the texts are careful that the flatness of that is not calm.

sequence.on_screen: Ten in the morning. Ground level, long lens, standing at the inside edge of the brick ring. The wall runs out of both sides of the frame as one flat horizontal line, bleached to two tones, with heat visibly rising off it. Held for a long time. Nothing in the frame moves except the air.
sequence.voice: This is a circle. From where this camera is standing there is no way to know that. It is about ninety metres across and about seven metres thick at the bottom, and somebody laid it, by hand, in brick and clay, with smaller rings inside it and a small square chamber at the middle. Nobody can tell you what it was for.

sequence.on_screen: One unbroken walking take at eye level, following the inside of the ring the whole way round. The wall does not change. The light does not change. The only evidence that anything has happened is the same broken course of brick coming back into frame at the end of the shot.
sequence.voice: There is a story attached to this, and it is worth saying exactly what the chronicle says and nothing more. A queen bore ten sons and one daughter. Brahmins skilled in the sacred texts looked at the daughter and foretold: for the sake of sovereignty will her son slay his uncles. The brothers resolved to kill their young sister, and the eldest of them, Abhaya, restrained them. And in due time they lodged her in a chamber having but one pillar, with a serving woman inside it and a hundred soldiers outside. The local name for this ring of brick means the house of one pillar.

sequence.on_screen: The citadel, a few hundred metres away, filmed square-on from a low position at midday so the whole frame is horizontal bands: dry grass, brick rampart, still water in the moat channel, brick again, white sky. No shadow anywhere in the frame.
sequence.voice: The chronicle finishes it in a few lines. A prince named Dighagamani heard of her, came, and got in at the window. A son was born and was carried out of the city the same day in a basket. Years later eight of the ten uncles marched against him and were killed, and the two who were spared were Abhaya, who had once stopped the others killing his sister, and the uncle whose daughter he had married. That is what the chronicle records: a sequence of events. It is not a law, and nothing on this ground shows that any of it had to happen. These films are not built on a machinery of desert, and the texts behind them do not issue verdicts on anybody's life.

sequence.on_screen: The interpretive board and the small departmental museum out at the road: a printed panel, a case of twelfth-century terracotta floor tiles with geese and elephants pressed into them, a coin. Then back to the ring for a wide static frame holding the whole visible arc, with one visitor walking away along it and out of shot.
sequence.voice: Every excavated thing here belongs to the twelfth century. The palace, the rampart, the moat, the tiles, the floor under the middle of the ring. The story belongs to the fifth century before Christ and to a city somewhere else whose site has never been agreed, and nothing has ever been found here that connects this ground to it. The name this place carries is a king's name from that earlier time; the bricks under the name are about seventeen hundred years younger. A former head of the island's archaeological service is said to have proposed something else entirely — that the ring is a model of the universe with a king installed at the centre of it. That proposal reaches us second-hand, in a travel handbook, with no reference and no argument attached, and it gets repeated anyway.

sequence.on_screen: Close and static on brick: the actual courses, salt bloom in the joints, moss, a root that has found a gap. Then one slow tilt up from the courses to the far side of the ring, which will not hold still.
sequence.voice: So a person standing here does not know what they are looking at. It is worth being exact about that, because it is easy to hear it as a fault and the commentaries do not. They separate two things that share a word. There is the doubt that counts as a hindrance, and it is narrow: wavering about eight specific matters — the teacher, the teaching, the community, moral conduct, the life before this one, the life after it, both together, and cause and effect [C008-P:L38–L58]. And there is the doubt that comes of thinking about something you do not know and cannot properly examine, and the text says plainly that this is not the hindrance doubt [C008-P:L36]. The other book gives that one a name of its own, look-alike doubt, and says it may not be unwholesome at all; it is simply something a mind does [C074-P:L404]. Not knowing what this is, is not the failure.

sequence.on_screen: The widest ground-level frame the site gives, then the same thing on a long lens: heat shimmer across the full width of the ring, the far wall dissolving and reassembling, brick compressed into vertical waver. The camera does not move at all.
sequence.voice: The failure they do describe is a different motion, and there is a picture of it in the air here. Unsettledness — the second of the two minds this film is about — is described as not subsiding, like a surface of water shaken by the wind; its work is not standing still, like a flag in wind; and the way it shows itself is scattering, like a heap of ash somebody has thrown a stone into [C074-P:L356]. It is set directly against calm [C074-P:L360]. The mechanism is precise. When a mind takes up an object, the power that holds it there until that mind ends is one-pointedness; agitation weakens that power, and then the other states arising with the mind are thrown off too and are given no room to take the object properly [C008-P:L62], so that a person cannot think steadily about a matter at all [C008-P:L64].

sequence.on_screen: Back at the citadel in the late afternoon, the light still hard. A slow pan along a hundred metres of rampart brick, then the palace floor, then a line of fallen brick that the department has sorted and stacked. The scale of what was made, filmed as labour rather than as grandeur: no low angle, no skyline, nothing looking up at anything.
sequence.voice: Which leaves the other half of this place, which is the work. Whatever the ring was, it was years of it, and somebody was certain enough about something to spend them. The compendium these films draw on has a whole vocabulary for that kind of certainty — a grip like a snake's on a frog [C074-P:L177], and among the four clingings it lists, the clinging to a view [C074-P:L196]. It would be easy to reach for that here and it would be wrong: the sources keep those items for a narrow set of positions about the way out of suffering, and they are not a licence to grade anybody's belief. What the second commentary does say, plainly, is that this kind of doubt grows in people who set out to settle matters lying outside the range of ordinary knowing, and in people who live on other people's confident talk about what comes after death [C008-M:L18]. That is not a warning against asking. It is a warning about the appetite for a verdict where nothing can be examined.

sequence.on_screen: The one aerial, and it is one continuous move. A vertical climb from inside the ring, holding the centre. At thirty metres it is still a wall. Higher, it starts to close. At the top of the climb the whole thing is a single clean circle with the small square foundation at its middle and the rectangle of the citadel and its moat off to one side of the frame. Then the same move in reverse, all the way back down to eye level, where it is a wall again and the shot ends.
sequence.voice: From up here you can measure it. You can see how round it is, how thick, how deliberate, and exactly where the middle is. You still cannot say what it was. The flat feeling that comes with that is worth naming, because the texts name it: in these states the feeling is neither pleasant nor painful, and the reason given is that a mind which has not got hold of its object can neither enjoy it nor dislike it [C008-P:L30]. They are careful that this greyness is not calm. Nothing has been settled here. A circle was drawn, a great deal was carried, a name was attached, and the ground has never agreed to any of it.

concept_merge.why_together:
C008 is the whole spine and that is why it leads. Read fresh, its two minds are not a matched pair of moods: delusion darkens a mind so that a matter cannot be known as it actually is, and it is dominant in two minds, the one joined with doubt and the one joined with restlessness [C008-M:L3]. The doubt half gives this film its subject twice over. Negatively, the Pradeepika restricts the harmful doubt to eight named matters [C008-P:L38] and states outright that doubt arising about something one does not know and cannot properly investigate is not the hindrance doubt [C008-P:L36]; the general definition it gives first is simply the inability to reach a decision about the object, and it is a hindrance because it blocks the wholesome [C008-P:L34]. Positively, the Margaya says where the harmful kind actually grows: in people who go to adjudicate matters lying outside the range of ordinary knowing, and in people who take in other people's empty talk about the hereafter, its remedy being confidence grounded in recognising the difference between oneself and a Buddha [C008-M:L18]. Those two statements, held together, are the film. A site whose name, board and fame all assert what its ground cannot confirm is a place where the honest gap is innocent and the appetite for a verdict is the thing under examination. The restlessness half then supplies the cinema: one-pointedness is the real power that holds a mind on its object until that mind ends, and when agitation weakens it the other states arising with the mind are thrown off and cannot take the object properly [C008-P:L62], so that steady thinking about a matter becomes impossible [C008-P:L64]. Both minds carry neutral feeling, because a mind that has not grasped its object can neither enjoy nor dislike it [C008-P:L25–L28; C008-P:L30].

C074 does three jobs C008 cannot. It supplies the images: unsettledness as a surface of water shaken by wind, a flag that will not stand still, a heap of ash struck by a stone, set directly against calm [C074-P:L356; C074-P:L360], which is literally what heat does to brick here between nine and three. It supplies the placement: these are hindrances, states that cover a mind and stop it taking the wholesome as its object at all [C074-P:L236], and doubt's own manifestation is listed as non-decision, with unwise attention as its proximate cause [C074-P:L402]. And it independently confirms the film's central distinction under its own term: hindrance doubt against look-alike doubt, ordinary uncertainty about an unknown matter, which it says may not be unwholesome and calls simply something that happens through a mass of mental operations [C074-P:L404]. That a second source, in a different chapter, draws the same line is what lets the film stand on it.

C074 also supplies the vocabulary this film deliberately declines to use. Its compendium contains the item that any careless writer would grab for here: clinging, described as holding an object without letting go, the way a snake holds a frog [C074-P:L177], of which one of four kinds is the clinging to a view [C074-P:L196], and among the knots the position that this alone is true and other roads are not [C074-P:L173]. The digest's limit is explicit — those warnings concern views taken as the road out of suffering and cannot be used on screen to judge or mock the religious or folk practice of real people — so the film names the item, says out loud that it does not fit here, and hands the weight back to C008-M:L18, which is about the appetite for verdicts rather than about anyone's faith. Naming the tool and refusing it is more honest than quietly using it.
concept_merge.what_it_reveals: That the two not-knowings on this ground are not the same thing, and that the sources rank them the opposite way round to how a documentary would. The modern visitor who cannot tell what the brick circle is is in the state the texts explicitly exempt. The interesting pressure is on the other side of the ground: the certainty that gets acted on. C008 alone would tempt a film into scolding the past, which the digest forbids twice over, since it says the source is not an argument against questioning and is equally not a slogan for healthy scepticism. C074 alone would leave a classification and a simile. Together they produce the only claim this film makes, which is that a monument can record an enormous quantity of certainty and still leave the question open, and that standing in front of that honestly is not a fault. The pairing also closes the two exits the film must not take. It cannot end in peace, because both digests say the flat neutrality of these states is not calm [C008-P:L30] and that unsettledness is precisely what calm stands against [C074-P:L360]. And it cannot end in debunking, because the sources are not asking whether the prediction was right; they are asking what a mind does when it settles a matter it has no way of examining.

concept_links.why:
The digest's account of doubt is what this location tests. Delusion darkens the mind so a matter cannot be known as it is, and is dominant in the two minds named here [C008-M:L3]; the general description of doubt is the inability to reach a decision about the object, and it is a hindrance because it obstructs the wholesome [C008-P:L34]; the harmful form is then restricted to eight named matters [C008-P:L38]; and the doubt of not knowing something and being unable to investigate it properly is stated not to be the hindrance doubt [C008-P:L36]. The Margaya locates the harmful kind's growth in going to adjudicate what lies beyond ordinary knowing and in absorbing other people's empty talk about the hereafter [C008-M:L18], and adds that these are the weakest of the unwholesome minds, doubt's particular harm being that it bends a person away from the wholesome and that good done with it is not strong good [C008-M:L16]. The restlessness half gives the mechanism and the film's visual logic: one-pointedness is the power that keeps a mind on its object until that mind ends, and agitation weakening it throws the rest off course [C008-P:L62], so steady thought about a matter becomes impossible [C008-P:L64]; both minds are neutral-feeling because an ungrasped object can be neither enjoyed nor disliked [C008-P:L25–L28; C008-P:L30].

Five limits from this digest are load-bearing here and are built into the design rather than noted at the end. It is not an argument against questioning, and the digest says so with a citation, so the film's central turn is the exemption rather than a reproach. It is equally not a slogan for healthy scepticism, so the film does not celebrate the archaeologists over the chronicle either; the remedy the Margaya gives is devotional and is not offered as this film's conclusion. The neutral feeling is not equanimity, which is why the last beat refuses to hear a measured circle as resolution. Weak does not mean harmless, so the unexplained ring is not played as a charming mystery. And restlessness is not a productivity problem with a mindfulness answer, since the source holds it present in every unwholesome mind, so the film offers no advice and no fix. The digest's own uncertainty is also honoured: it records that the Pradeepika does not spell out how its general definition of doubt relates to the restricted eight, and that this needs expert checking before any film states what counts as harmful doubt — so the narration quotes the restriction and the exemption and draws no further boundary of its own.

The compendium supplies the images, the placement and, decisively, an independent second statement of the distinction the film turns on. Unsettledness is characterised as not subsiding, like a water surface shaken by wind; its function is not standing still, like a flag in wind; its manifestation is scattering, like a heap of ash struck by a stone; and its proximate cause is unwise attention [C074-P:L356]. Unsettledness and remorse are counted one hindrance because their function, condition and opposite are the same, the condition being the turning over of past misfortunes and the opposite being calm [C074-P:L360]. Hindrances are defined as what covers over and blocks, keeping a mind from taking the wholesome and Nibbāna as its object [C074-P:L236]; doubt's listed manifestation is non-decision, with unwise attention again as proximate cause [C074-P:L402]. And the Pradeepika here divides doubt in two: the hindrance kind, about the eight matters, against look-alike doubt, which arises about a matter one does not know and which it says may not be unwholesome, being simply an activity carried out through a mass of mental operations [C074-P:L404]. That is the film's hinge, and having it in two separate chapters of two separate books is why the film is willing to build on it.

The digest's limits shape what this link is allowed to do. The warnings about rites-and-rituals and about the position that this alone is true concern views taken as the path to liberation and cannot be used on screen to judge or mock real people's religious or folk practice — so although the film names clinging [C074-P:L177], the clinging to a view [C074-P:L196] and the this-alone-is-true knot [C074-P:L173], it names them in order to say that they do not fit this ground, and the weight of the argument is carried by C008-M:L18 instead. Abandonment in these sources is staged and technical rather than a decision, so no beat suggests that anyone could have let go of anything. The stakes in the source are rebirth and world-ages rather than stress or wellbeing, so no wellbeing language appears anywhere in the narration. The aids the text lists against unsettledness and remorse are strikingly ordinary — much hearing, asking many questions, familiarity with the training, keeping company with elders, good friends, and talk suitable to the occasion [C074-P:L366–L380] — which is a further reason the film gives no instruction: there is nothing heroic on offer to dramatise. One more item is available and is held back deliberately: the latent tendencies, which are said to be apt to rise again whenever a suitable object is obtained [C074-P:L474] and whose existence is not manifest until an occasion brings it up [C074-M:L71], would make a neat figure for a claim sleeping inside a place name until somebody reads the board. The digest warns that such figures are editorial and must not be presented as scriptural, so it stays in this field and out of the voice.

what_the_viewer_could_understand: That there are two completely different things people call not knowing, and that the old commentaries are careful to separate them. Standing in front of something and honestly being unable to say what it is, is explicitly not the fault they list; one of them even gives that state its own name and says it may not be a fault at all. What they do warn about is the appetite for a verdict on matters nothing can examine — and this is a place where a great deal of brick was carried on the strength of one, where the board still explains it, and where the ground has never confirmed any of it. Also that the flat, grey feeling of an open question is not peace. The texts say so in as many words.
what_must_be_real: The ruin, the heat, the shimmer, the measurements and the disagreement. Nothing is arranged, cleared, wetted, lit or reconstructed: no brick is moved or restacked for a frame, no vegetation is cut, no board is cleaned or re-lettered, and the ring is filmed at whatever state of conservation it is actually in. The shimmer is real heat on real brick and is never added, and the aerial shows the circle as it is, with no straightening, stitching or completion of the arc where the ring is broken. The dating and the disagreements are stated as the published record states them, and where a figure is reported inconsistently the film uses the figure the sources agree on and says nothing it cannot support. The woman in the chronicle is a chronicle figure and stays one: her confinement is not dramatised, reconstructed, re-enacted or scored, no frame lingers on the ring as a cell, nothing is imagined about her state of mind, and no shot is composed from a point of view inside it. Her brother is not narrated as cruel, her son is not narrated as fated, and the child appears as one clause of a chronicle summary and nothing else. No child appears in the film. The temple a hundred metres away is in use and the film stays outside its precinct: no act of worship is filmed, interrupted, restarted or lit, and no monk, worshipper or temple worker is filmed at all. Visitors appear only as distant figures giving scale, never held long enough to become a subject, never framed as puzzled, credulous or instructed, and never filmed where a face is legible without consent freely given. If the site's custodians or the temple would rather the crew were not there, the film does not happen.
position_hint: Middle to late in the group, and specifically after the film that draws the line between an honest gap in the evidence and the state the sources actually warn about. That film establishes the boundary in the present tense, on a decision somebody has to make this morning. This one shows the far side of the same boundary at the scale of a thousand years and a monument: what it looks like when a matter beyond examination gets settled anyway and then built. It also needs to come before the group's closing film about speed, because this one leaves the question open on purpose and the closing film is the one allowed to resolve. No location reasoning is involved in the placement.
risks: Becoming a film about a false prophecy, or about superstition. This is the single most likely failure and the digests do not license it: the sources are not asking whether a prediction was correct, the Pradeepika explicitly exempts honest uncertainty from the fault it names, and the C008 digest states that the material is neither an argument against questioning nor a slogan for healthy scepticism. The narration never asserts that the prediction was false and never invites the viewer to feel superior to anyone in the chronicle.

Narrating the prophecy's fulfilment as destiny, desert, or a universe putting things right. Kamma is not fate. Beat 3 exists to refuse this in the voice, and the chronicle's own sequence is given as a sequence with the refusal attached.

Turning the woman in the chronicle into a character, a victim or an object of pity. She is a figure in a chronicle summary. Any reconstruction, any interiority, any shot framed as her view, any lingering on the ring as a cell, and the film has broken its own floor.

Making the archaeologists the heroes and the chronicle the villain, which is the mirror image of the first risk and just as wrong. The film records layers and does not adjudicate between them, and the one scholarly alternative it mentions is itself unsupported by any published argument.

Using the compendium's clinging-to-a-view item to grade the belief of people in the chronicle or of people at the site today. The C074 digest forbids exactly this. The film names the item and says out loud that it does not apply.
Hearing the last beat as resolution or serenity. A measured circle is still an unexplained circle, and both digests say the flatness of these states is not calm.

Quoting the site's own signage or the popular accounts as fact. Three separate numbers in circulation here are unreliable: the figure of 297 feet is published as a circumference by one source and as a diameter by another, the uncle count is given as nine in most retellings where the chronicle itself gives eight killed of ten, and the excavation start date is given as both 1934 and 1947. Every one of them is the kind of borrowed fact this project has been caught by before.

Naming the place. The monument's own name is a place name in effect, and so is the site's name, which is built out of a king's name. The voice refers to the monument by what its name means and refers to the site's name only as a king's name from a named century, without saying whose.

Aerial permission. This is an archaeological protected site, the aerial is the film's one resolution, and the reported altitude ceiling for general drone operation is lower than the height the circle needs to close at. A refusal or a low ceiling costs the payoff, not the film.

Physical conditions. The whole film is shot in the hottest hours on open ground with no shade over the rampart or the ring, and one beat is a continuous walk of nearly three hundred metres carrying a camera in that heat. Water, timing and a shorter working day matter more here than kit.
drop_if: The ring cannot be walked and filmed without stepping on or destabilising brickwork, or the department's conditions rule out ground access inside the earthwork. The walking take is the film's spine and the fallback for a refused aerial; without it there is no film.
The site's custodians or the neighbouring temple would rather the crew were not there, or filming cannot happen without visitors and worshippers being in frame in a way that makes them the subject.

The shimmer does not read. The whole treatment rests on heat behaving visibly on brick through the middle of the day, and if a pre-visit in the dry months shows the effect is weak at the scale of this wall, the film's look has no engine and a different site type should carry the concept.
The circular structure has been re-roofed, fenced off, re-turfed or interpretively rebuilt since the published accounts, which would remove both the geometry and the honest ambiguity.

connections.note: That film draws the line between an honest gap in the evidence and the state the sources warn about, in the present tense and on a decision someone must make now. This one stands on the far side of the same line, at the scale of a monument and a thousand years.
A place where three different answers are all correct, against a place where one answer is asserted everywhere and nothing can confirm it.
An open question left open on hard flat ground in vertical light, handing over to the group's closing film about how fast to go when you can honestly only see this far.

selection.reason: It is the only ruin in the group, the only film whose subject is a claim attached to a structure, and the only one whose philosophy comes from documented history rather than from resemblance. It is also the film that breaks the group's monoculture: nine of the eleven candidates were working or natural places carrying the concepts by analogy, and a group cannot be a monoculture.

review.note: Rewritten completely on 2026-09-25 and the verdict reset, because the body is new: the film is no longer a night wholesale vegetable terminal but a ruined twelfth-century citadel and the great circular brick earthwork beside it. The reason for the replacement is the monoculture rule. Nine of this group's eleven candidates were working places or natural landforms carrying C008 and C074 by analogy — a reservoir drawdown, a marsh, a surf coast, grazing circles, a night dansala road, charcoal pits, curd pots, a seedling hillside and a mountain railway — and Chathura has ruled that a group cannot be a monoculture, so the weakest occupant of the crowded cell was replaced with the group's only ruin, its only medieval royal site, and its only film about a claim attached to a structure. The treatment is also new and is shared with nothing else in the group: vertical midday light, heat shimmer, flat plan-drawing geometry, a static camera, and one single continuous vertical move as the whole payoff. The film is now bound to a verified historical story. The Mahavamsa records that brahmins skilled in the sacred texts foretold that a king's youngest daughter would bear a son who would slay his uncles for the sake of sovereignty, that the brothers resolved to kill her and the eldest restrained them, that they lodged her in a chamber having but one pillar with a serving woman inside and a hundred soldiers outside, that she bore a son by prince Dighagamani who was carried out at birth, and that eight of the ten uncles were later killed. The colossal circular earthwork at the site is popularly held to be the base of that tower and the local name means the house of one pillar — and no archaeological evidence has been found linking the site to that period at all, everything excavated being twelfth-century, so the site is very probably not the ancient capital its name claims. Three claims this project would have inherited were corrected by the research and are held in what_is_disputed rather than used: the prophecy in Geiger's translation names no number of uncles and the chronicle records eight killed of ten rather than nine, the confinement is done by the brothers under their father's reign rather than by one brother after his own consecration, and the widely quoted 297 feet is published as a circumference by one source and as a diameter by another, only the diameter reading being consistent with the independently reported ninety metres. Citations were re-tested line by line against both digests, and the film's hinge — that honest uncertainty about an unexamined matter is explicitly not the doubt on the list of faults — is carried at C008-P:L36 and independently at C074-P:L404. A new proposed location with a full historical thread replaces the old one.

suggested_location.region: Kurunegala District, North Western Province: low inland country at Kottambapitiya, about 2.5 km east of Hettipola on the B79, roughly halfway between Kurunegala and Chilaw and some 19 km from Wariyapola. This is the district's northern, drier end, in the island's dry-to-intermediate agro-ecological transition, where drought is a normal feature rather than the wet-zone hill country further south.
suggested_location.why_here: Because the concept does not have to be staged here: the disagreement is the site. This is a genuine medieval royal citadel — a square brick rampart and a broad moat around a palace whose ground plan matches the Polonnaruwa palace, with an east gateway, a Nissankamalla slab inscription confirming the complex was in good order in the 1190s, and a Tamil inscription found in 1951 — and it is also the site of one structure that nothing on the island resembles: a circular earthwork of brick and clay about ninety metres across, seven metres thick at the base, with concentric clay rings and a small square-chambered foundation at the centre. Around that circle sit a name, a famous chronicle story, a board, a popular identification and at least four scholarly or semi-scholarly proposals, and the published position is that no archaeological evidence has ever been found to support any of them, while the whole excavated assemblage — palace, rampart, moat, floor tiles, the floor under the centre of the ring — is twelfth-century, about seventeen hundred years younger than the story the place is named for. That is C008's own distinction standing on real ground: an enormous quantity of certainty, spent; and a modern visitor in a state of honest not-knowing that the sources specifically exempt from the fault they name. The cinema is in the same place as the argument. The ring is too large to be seen from inside it, so it reads at eye level as a flat wall and resolves into a circle only from the air or by walking it, which makes the film's best shot and its clearest statement the same shot. And dry-season brick under vertical sun gives heat shimmer across a ninety-metre span — the compendium's own image for unsettledness, a surface that will not stand still, available as real weather on a real wall.

historical_thread.story:
Two stories sit on this ground and they are separated by about seventeen centuries.

The first is in the chronicle. The Mahavamsa, compiled in the fifth or sixth century CE, gives it in chapter IX, 'The Consecrating of Abhaya'. In Geiger's standard translation the queen of Panduvasudeva 'bore ten sons and one daughter: the eldest of all was named Abhaya, the youngest (child, the) daughter was named Cittā. When the brahmans skilled in sacred texts saw her they foretold: "For the sake of sovereignty will her son slay his uncles." When the brothers resolved: "let us kill our young sister," Abhaya restrained them.' Then: 'In due time they lodged her in a chamber having but one pillar, and the entry thereto they made through the king's sleeping chamber; and within they placed a serving woman, and a hundred soldiers without. But since she (Citta) drove men mad by the mere sight of her beauty, the name given to her was lengthened by an epithet "Ummadacitta".' Dighagamani, son of prince Dighayu, 'heard of Ummadacitta' and 'went, driven by longing for her, to Upatissagama'; her attendant 'fastened a hookladder to the window in the night, climbed up, broke the window and so came in'. When she became pregnant the king proposed marriage and his sons agreed, 'saying: "If it is a son we will slay him"'. She arranged for another woman near her own delivery; she bore a son and the other a daughter; the son and a thousand pieces of money were handed over and the daughter laid beside her, and the king's sons, hearing that a daughter had been born, 'were well pleased'. The boy was named Panduabhaya, after his grandfather and his eldest uncle. Chapter X takes him through three attempts on his life, a brahman teacher named Pandula, an army, a marriage and years of war: 'Eight of his uncles, leaving two behind, drew near to the Arittha-mountain in battle array'; his men 'killed all the soldiers of the enemy's army and the eight uncles with them, and they raised a pyramid of skulls'. He spared two — Abhaya, 'because his mother and he himself had been befriended by him', who was made nagaraguttika, guardian of the city, and his father-in-law Girikandasiva, who kept his district. The chronicle sets the confinement at Upatissagama, a city whose site has never been agreed.

The second story is the ground. What is actually here is a ruined royal complex of about twenty hectares, declared an archaeological reserve by gazette on 30 April 1931 and systematically excavated from the middle of the twentieth century. It is identified as Parakramapura, capital of the principality of Dakkhinadesa, the seat from which Parakramabahu I ruled as sub-king from about 1140 before taking the whole island in 1153. The royal quarter is a nearly square enclosure of roughly 310 by 330 metres, reported elsewhere as 1056 by 990 feet, ringed by a moat about 16 metres wide and a brick rampart about 2.5 metres thick at the base and half that above, with the gateway to the east between two brick platforms and a passage about 12 feet wide; the wall on the north-east was built to let a sheet of water in and form a pond. The palace inside measures about 108 by 100 metres, its central building about 36 by 27 metres around an open court, and its ground plan follows Parakramabahu's palace at Polonnaruwa. A slab inscription of Nissankamalla (1187–1196) records the complex in good condition at his visit; a Tamil inscription found in 1951 records the deeds of a commander of the same reign. Terracotta floor tiles from the inner court, stamped with elephants and hamsa geese, are in museum collections. There is a departmental archaeological museum on the road, first set up in the 1970s and moved into its present building in 1983, holding statuary, stone, metal, terracotta, coins including pieces with Greek characters and Chinese currency of the tenth to thirteenth centuries, pottery and jewellery. Beside the site stands Panduwasnuwara Raja Maha Vihara, a working temple declared an archaeological site on 13 March 1970, with a Kandyan-period tampita image house on sixteen granite stumps, a dalada maligaya of 22 granite pillars on a five-foot platform, a bodhi tree with a pillar inscription, and ninth-century inscriptions.

And about a hundred metres from that temple is the thing the place is famous for. Inside a circular earthwork — a ring of brick and clay reported at about 90 metres across and about 7 metres thick at the base, with a series of concentric clay walls inside it and a small square chamber at the very centre, its floor laid with granite slabs — nothing has ever been securely explained. Local tradition says it is the base of the one-pillared tower of the chronicle, and the name it carries, Ektam Ge, means the house of one pillar. Excavation of the floor at the centre found what is taken to be a representation of Mount Meru under the granite slabs, and dated it, like everything else here, to the twelfth century. Paranavitana, the former Archaeological Commissioner, is reported to have held that the whole thing is the mythical cakravāḷa, the rim of the world, with Parakramabahu I installed at the centre as Cakravarti, lord of the universe; that report reaches print without a reference or a supporting argument. Other readings have been floated and discarded — an arena, though the brick slopes have neither steps nor benches; a great pond, though a pond would be dug down rather than banked up at ground level and would not have a building in the middle of it; a separate circular citadel outside the rectangular one, on the strength of the folk name Biso Kotuwa. The blunt published summary is that there is no archaeological evidence to prove any of the stories, and none has ever been found here connecting this ground to the fifth century BC at all.
historical_thread.how_it_binds:
C008's doubt has an inside edge and an outside edge, and this site puts something different on each of them. That is why the location is right rather than merely apt.

The outside edge first, because it is the one a careless film would get wrong. The Pradeepika defines doubt generally as the inability to reach a decision about its object and calls it a hindrance because it blocks the wholesome [C008-P:L34], then restricts the harmful kind to eight named matters [C008-P:L38], and then says something a film can actually use: the doubt that arises when a person thinks about something they do not know and cannot properly investigate is not the hindrance doubt [C008-P:L36]. The compendium says it again in its own chapter and gives the state a name, look-alike doubt, adding that it may not be unwholesome at all and is simply something carried out through a mass of mental operations [C074-P:L404]. A visitor standing in front of this brick ring is exactly there. The board says one thing, the excavation report says another, the name says a third, four proposals contradict each other and one of them has no published argument behind it. There is no available decision. The film's central claim is therefore an exemption, not a reproach, and the site is the clearest place in the country to earn it: the not-knowing is not the visitor's failing, it is a property of the ground.

The inside edge is where the labour comes in. The Margaya says where the harmful kind of doubt grows: in people who set out to adjudicate matters lying outside the range of ordinary knowing, and in people who take in the empty talk others make about the world after death [C008-M:L18]. A prediction about a child not yet conceived is precisely a matter of that kind, and this place is what such a matter looks like when it is acted on at scale — a ring ninety metres across, laid course by course, by people certain enough to spend years on it, for a reason nobody can now recover. The binding is exact and it is not a debunking: the source is not interested in whether the brahmans were right. It is interested in what a mind is doing when it reaches a verdict on something it has no way of examining, and in the traffic in such verdicts, which is what has accumulated on this ring for a thousand years and is still accumulating on the board. The Margaya's own remedy is confidence grounded in recognising the difference between oneself and a Buddha — a devotional position, and the digest says so, which is another reason the film ends without a recommendation.

The history also supplies the film's refusal of fate, which the floor requires. The prophecy was fulfilled; the chronicle says so. But the chronicle records a sequence, not a mechanism, and the record actively resists the tidy reading. The number in Geiger's text is no number at all: 'For the sake of sovereignty will her son slay his uncles.' The count that everyone repeats, nine of ten, is not what the chronicle delivers — eight of the ten were killed and two were spared, and one of the two spared was Abhaya, the brother who had stopped the others killing her in the first place, spared for exactly that reason. A story in which the man who protected her survives, and in which the prediction as translated names no total while the outcome misses the total everyone quotes, is not a story about destiny closing over people. It is a story about a prediction, a very great deal of effort, and a set of events, with no demonstrable line drawn between them. Kamma is not fate, and here the record itself declines to make it one.

Then C074 turns the whole thing into pictures. Unsettledness is not subsiding, like a surface of water shaken by the wind; its work is not standing still, like a flag in wind; it shows itself as scattering, like a heap of ash a stone has been thrown into; and its proximate cause is unwise attention [C074-P:L356]. It is set directly against calm [C074-P:L360]. On this ground, in the dry months, between nine in the morning and three in the afternoon, a ninety-metre brick wall in vertical sun does that: the far side of the ring genuinely will not stand still. The hindrances are defined as what covers a mind and keeps it from taking the wholesome as its object at all [C074-P:L236], and the ring does the covering physically as well — it is so large that from inside it the shape is invisible, and the Pradeepika's mechanism explains why the eye gets no purchase: one-pointedness is the power that holds a mind on an object until that mind ends, agitation weakens it and throws the accompanying states off, and then nothing can take the object properly [C008-P:L62] and steady thought about the matter becomes impossible [C008-P:L64]. The aerial is the one moment the object is taken whole, and the film immediately concedes that taking it whole answers nothing, which is where the neutral feeling belongs: not pleasant, not painful, because an ungrasped object can be neither enjoyed nor disliked [C008-P:L30], and explicitly not calm.

Finally, C074 supplies something the film deliberately does not use, and the history is why that matters. The compendium's clinging is a grip that does not let the object go, like a snake's on a frog [C074-P:L177]; one of the four kinds is the clinging to a view [C074-P:L196]; and among the knots is the position that this alone is true and other roads are not [C074-P:L173]. A film about a prophecy and a signboard would reach for those instantly. The digest closes it: those warnings concern views taken as the road out of suffering and cannot be used on screen to judge or mock real people's religious or folk practice. The people who laid this brick are not available to be graded, the people who maintain the temple next door are not on trial, and the tradition that the ring is the one-pillared tower is somebody's living local knowledge. So the film names the items, says they do not fit, and leaves the weight on C008-M:L18, which is about the appetite for verdicts rather than about anybody's faith.
what_is_certain: The site is an archaeological reserve of about twenty hectares at Kottambapitiya, about 2.5 km east of Hettipola on the B79, in Kurunegala District, North Western Province. It was declared a reserve by gazette notification published on 30 April 1931.
The great majority of the excavated remains, including the palace, the rampart, the moat and the terracotta floor tiles, are dated to the twelfth century CE.
The site is identified with Parakramapura, capital of the principality of Dakkhinadesa, the seat from which Parakramabahu I ruled as sub-king from about 1140 before unifying the island in 1153.

The royal residential quarter is a nearly square enclosure, reported as about 310 by 330 metres and also as 1056 by 990 feet, enclosed by a moat about 16 metres wide and a brick rampart about 2.5 metres thick at the base, reduced by about half at the upper levels. The gateway is on the east side, between two brick platforms set at right angles to the citadel, with a passage about 12 feet wide. The north-east wall was built so as to admit a sheet of water and form a pond.
The palace measures about 108 by 100 metres, with a central building of about 36 by 27 metres around an open court, and its ground plan resembles Parakramabahu's palace at Polonnaruwa.

A slab inscription of Nissankamalla (1187–1196) records that the palace complex was in good condition at the time of his visit. A Tamil inscription discovered in 1951 records the deeds of a commander of the same reign.

There is a separate circular earthwork on the site, a ring of brick and clay, containing a small circular or square-chambered foundation at its centre whose floor is laid with granite slabs, with concentric clay walls between the outer ring and the centre. Nothing comparable in size is known from the rest of the island's ancient architecture.
Excavation of the floor at the centre of that structure recovered what is interpreted as a representation of Mount Meru beneath the granite slabs, and it too is dated to the twelfth century.

The structure is known locally as Ektam Ge or Ektem Maligaya, as Chakrawala Kotuwa, and as Biso Kotuwa, and local tradition holds it to be the tower in which the princess of the chronicle was confined.

The published position on that tradition is that no archaeological evidence has been found to support it. Wikipedia states flatly that 'there is no archaeological evidence to prove such stories', and Lankapradeepa that 'no single archaeological evidence has been found so far from this site to prove that belief'. Lankapradeepa also states that 'the remains excavated within this ancient city have not yielded any archaeological evidence to connect the site with the hoary times of King Panduvasudeva'.

The Mahavamsa, chapter IX, in Geiger's translation as published at lakdiva.org.lk, records that the queen 'bore ten sons and one daughter: the eldest of all was named Abhaya, the youngest (child, the) daughter was named Cittā', that 'when the brahmans skilled in sacred texts saw her they foretold: "For the sake of sovereignty will her son slay his uncles"', that 'when the brothers resolved: "let us kill our young sister," Abhaya restrained them', and that 'in due time they lodged her in a chamber having but one pillar, and the entry thereto they made through the king's sleeping chamber; and within they placed a serving woman, and a hundred soldiers without'.

The same chapter records that Dighagamani, son of prince Dighayu, went to Upatissagama on hearing of her; that her attendant 'fastened a hookladder to the window in the night, climbed up, broke the window and so came in'; that the king's sons consented to a marriage 'saying: "If it is a son we will slay him"'; that she exchanged her newborn son for another woman's newborn daughter along with a thousand pieces of money; and that the boy was named Panduabhaya after his grandfather and his eldest uncle.

Mahavamsa chapter X records that 'eight of his uncles, leaving two behind, drew near to the Arittha-mountain in battle array', that the prince's men 'killed all the soldiers of the enemy's army and the eight uncles with them, and they raised a pyramid of skulls', that he did not slay Abhaya 'because his mother and he himself had been befriended by him' but made him nagaraguttika, guardian of the city, and that he did not slay his father-in-law Girikandasiva but handed him the district of Girikanda.
The chronicle places the confinement and these events at Upatissagama.

A departmental archaeological museum stands on the road at Kotampitiya junction on the Kurunegala–Chilaw road. It was first established in the 1970s and moved in 1983 into a building acquired by the department, and it serves as the regional archaeological institution for the North Western Province. Its holdings include statuary, stone, metal and terracotta objects, coins and pottery and jewellery from excavation, donation and court orders.

Panduwasnuwara Raja Maha Vihara stands beside the site and was declared an archaeological site on 13 March 1970. It has a Kandyan-period tampita image house standing on sixteen granite stumps with a mandapa on six pillars and Kandyan-style murals, a dalada maligaya about 50 by 30 feet on a five-foot granite platform with 22 granite pillars, sixteen stone pillars carrying inscriptions of the Anuradhapura period including ones of Udaya II (887–898), and a bodhi tree with a pillar inscription. Reported accounts place the circular structure about 100 metres from the temple.
Older local names for the overgrown site were Nuwara-kele, the forest of the city, and Agala-kele Mukalana, the forest of the moat.

Kurunegala District spans nine agro-ecological regions of the dry and intermediate zones with a negligible wet-zone portion, and drought is a common feature of the district's northern parts, where this site lies.
what_is_disputed: The identification of the site with the capital its name claims. The name refers to a king of the fifth century BC, and the excavated remains do not reach that period at all; Lankapradeepa states that the excavated remains 'have not yielded any archaeological evidence to connect the site with the hoary times of King Panduvasudeva'. The chronicle itself places the episode at Upatissagama, a city whose location has never been agreed by anyone. The film does not assert that the site is or is not that capital; it records that the name makes a claim the ground does not support.

What the circular structure actually was. At least five readings are in circulation and not one of them is established. Local tradition: the base of the one-pillared tower of the chronicle. Paranavitana, reported second-hand: the mythical cakravāḷa or rim of the world, with Parakramabahu I installed at the centre as Cakravarti, lord of the universe — a claim that reaches print in a 1974 travel handbook with no reference and no supporting argument, a caveat that the handbook's own author records. A separate circular citadel outside the rectangular one, on the strength of the folk name Biso Kotuwa, a word that elsewhere means a sluice valve-pit. An arena, which is rejected because the brick slopes have neither steps nor benches. A great pond, which is rejected because a pond would be excavated downward rather than banked at ground level and would not contain a building at its centre. The Mount Meru representation found under the granite slabs at the centre is compatible with the cosmological reading and does not by itself establish it.

The historicity of the chronicle episode itself. The prophecy, the confinement, the hook-ladder, the substituted infant and the pyramid of skulls are chronicle narrative, compiled roughly a thousand years after the events they describe, and nothing excavated anywhere bears on them. This is recorded as what the chronicles say, never as what happened.

The number of uncles in the prophecy and in the outcome. Almost every popular account, including the site literature, says the brahmans foretold that her son would kill nine of his ten uncles. Geiger's translation of Mahavamsa IX gives no number at all: 'For the sake of sovereignty will her son slay his uncles.' Mahavamsa X then records eight of the ten killed in battle and two spared, Abhaya and Girikandasiva. At least one popular account says eight. The Dipavamsa also carries the episode and was not read in this research. The film uses the chronicle's own figures and does not use the number nine.

Who confined her, and when. Popular accounts, including the ones that supplied this project's brief, say that one brother, once consecrated king, shut his sister in the tower. Geiger's Mahavamsa says the brothers collectively lodged her in the chamber during their father's reign, that the brother who later became king is the one who restrained the others from killing her, and that Abhaya was consecrated only after Panduvasudeva's death, which the chronicle places after the boy's birth. The popular accounts also inflate the guard: the chronicle says one serving woman within and a hundred soldiers without, not hundreds guarding day and night, and the chamber has a window that a man climbs through. The film follows the chronicle and does not follow the retellings.

The dimensions of the circular structure, and specifically the figure of 297 feet. AmazingLanka states that 'the base measures 297 feet in circumference'. Another account gives a clay wall '21 feet at the base' with 'a diameter of 297 feet'. An independent description gives the circular rampart as 90 metres in diameter and almost 7 metres wide at the base. 297 feet is 90.5 metres, and 21 feet is 6.4 metres, so the diameter reading is consistent with the independent figures while the circumference reading would imply a ring only about 29 metres across. The working figures for the film are therefore about 90 metres across and about 7 metres thick at the base, with the circumference at roughly 280 metres, and the discrepancy is recorded rather than resolved. A third figure, a 3.3 metre diameter with a circular garden marked 40 metres out, evidently describes the small structure at the centre rather than the ring, and has not been reconciled with the rest.

When systematic excavation began. One account says excavations began in 1934 under Senarath Paranavitana; another says systematic work began in 1947, with most of the scientific research done after independence. Both are reported; neither was verified against a departmental report.

Whether the circular earthwork is surrounded by a moat of its own. One account describes 'an ektemge (circular tower) surrounded by a circular moat'; another describes only a circular earthwork rampart on ground level and explicitly argues against reading the interior as water. To be checked on the ground before the beat that films flat water is written into a plan.

The etymology of the monument's name. It is glossed as the house of one pillar or pillar-house, after the Mahavamsa's 'chamber having but one pillar', and separately as 'ivory tower'. The first is consistent with the chronicle wording in Geiger; the second appears without support. The film uses only the first, and refers to the monument by what the name means rather than by the name.

The number of storeys and the internal plan of the supposed tower. One account states that within the innermost wall was a square chamber and that the tower is believed to have had several storeys. Nothing found in this research supports the storeys as an excavated finding rather than an inference from the legend.

Above all: none of this adjudicates anything, and the film does not adjudicate it. What the record establishes is what has been excavated and dated, and what has been asserted, by whom, and on what evidence. It establishes that the assertions about this ring are not supported and that the site's own name is not supported. It establishes nothing about whether a prediction made in a chronicle was correct, and the film does not raise that question. Where the identification of a structure or a site is contested, that it is contested is the finding.

what_to_film: The opening frame: ground level at the inside edge of the brick ring, long lens, mid-morning, the wall running out of both edges as a flat line with heat coming off it. Held long. This is the shot that establishes that the subject cannot be seen.

The circuit: one unbroken walking take at eye level all the way round the inside of the ring, roughly 280 metres, with the same broken course of brick returning at the end. This is the film's spine and the fallback if the aerial is refused.
The small square-chambered foundation at the dead centre of the ring, filmed flat and plainly, with the granite slabs of its floor.
The concentric clay rings between the outer ring and the centre, wherever they are legible at ground level, filmed as bands rather than as objects.
The citadel square-on from a low position at noon: horizontal bands of dry grass, brick rampart, still water in the moat, brick and white sky, with no shadow anywhere in frame.
The east gateway between its two brick platforms, and the palace floor plan with its open central court, shot from the ground rather than from above so it reads as a plan the eye has to assemble.
Extreme close texture on brick: courses, salt bloom, moss in the joints, a root in a gap, tool marks if any survive. The film needs one sequence of surfaces to earn its scale.
The heat shimmer itself, twice: the widest ground-level frame the site gives, and the same span on a long lens so the far wall compresses into vertical waver. Camera locked off both times.
The interpretive board and the museum at the road: the printed panel, the twelfth-century terracotta floor tiles with elephants and hamsa geese, a coin. Filmed as documents, not as treasures.
Visitors only as distant scale: a single figure arriving at the board, reading, looking at the ring and walking out of frame. No face legible, nobody followed, nobody's expression used.

The one aerial, if permitted, as a single continuous vertical climb from inside the ring holding the centre, up to the height at which the ring closes and the rectangle of the citadel and its moat enters frame, then the identical move in reverse back down to eye level. The whole payoff is the rise and the fall as one shot.
Deliberately not filmed: the working temple's precinct, any act of worship, any monk, worshipper or temple worker, and any dawn or dusk material.
suggested_location.access: Easy to reach and physically open. The site is on the B79 about 2.5 km east of Hettipola, roughly halfway between Kurunegala and Chilaw and about 40 km from Kurunegala; a small museum with a ticket booth sits at the road. Ground access to the ruins is on foot over open, level ground with almost no shade. What is not simple is permission. This is an archaeological protected site under the Department of Archaeology, so filming is a departmental matter and every condition in a permission letter binds the crew; a commercial filming fee is reported at the order of Rs 25,000 per site per week, unverified. Any aerial work needs drone registration and a permit from the Civil Aviation Authority of Sri Lanka and, separately, clearance from the Department of Archaeology, and reported general conditions are daylight only, within visual line of sight, and not above about 100 feet unless higher altitude is specifically permitted. That ceiling is the live problem: a ring about 90 metres across will not close into a circle at 30 metres of altitude, so the ask includes the higher-altitude exemption and the film should be planned on the assumption that it may not come. The honest fallback is already in the design — the walking circuit at eye level is the film's spine and the resolution can be lost without losing the piece, which would then end on the shimmer rather than on the shape. The working temple beside the site is separately declared and is in use; the film stays outside its precinct and does not rely on its permission. Nothing here has been verified with the department, the authority, the site's custodians or the temple.
suggested_location.best_time: The dry, clear, hard part of the year, roughly late January to March, before the inter-monsoon storms and before April's heat makes a 280-metre walking take with a camera unsafe. Within the day, nine in the morning to about three in the afternoon: vertical light, bleached brick, no modelling, maximum shimmer. A single late-afternoon block is wanted for the rampart pan in beat 7, where long flat shadows across open ground read as distance rather than as beauty. No dawn, no dusk, no golden hour anywhere in the film. If the aerial is permitted it wants the same midday light as the ground work, because a low sun would model the ring into something prettier and less legible.

suggested_location.research_note:
All of this is desk research by web search and none of it has been checked on the ground, against a printed edition, or with any authority. The chronicle passages are Geiger's translation of the Mahavamsa as published at lakdiva.org.lk, chapters IX and X, read in full and quoted from there rather than from a print edition; the Dipavamsa, which carries the same episode, was not read. The site's dating, identification, measurements, inscriptions, museum and temple detail come from the sources listed and were cross-read between at least two of them wherever possible, and where they disagree the disagreement is recorded in what_is_disputed and is not resolved.

Three claims this project would otherwise have inherited were checked and corrected. First, the prophecy: the version in general circulation, including the site literature, has the brahmans foretelling that her son would slay nine of his ten uncles, and Geiger's text gives no number, while chapter X records eight of the ten killed and two spared. Second, the confinement: the popular accounts have one brother, already consecrated king, shutting his sister away, and the chronicle has the brothers doing it collectively during their father's reign, has Abhaya restraining the others from killing her, and has his consecration come after the boy's birth; the popular accounts also inflate a hundred soldiers into hundreds guarding day and night and drop the window the chronicle explicitly gives the chamber. Third, the measurement: 297 feet is published as a circumference by AmazingLanka and as a diameter by another account, and only the diameter reading is consistent with the independently reported 90-metre diameter and 7-metre base, so the figures used here are about 90 metres across, about 7 metres thick at the base, and roughly 280 metres around, with the discrepancy recorded rather than smoothed. A further reported figure, a 3.3-metre diameter with a circular garden marked 40 metres out, appears to describe the small central structure and is not reconciled with the rest.

The Paranavitana cakravāḷa interpretation could not be traced to a publication by Paranavitana himself. It reaches this research through Lankapradeepa and through a discussion of a 1974 travel handbook whose own author notes that no reference or argument is given for the claim, and it is recorded as reported rather than as scholarship. The rejections of the arena, pond and circular-citadel readings are one author's reasoning on a commercial travel site, are stated as that, and would need checking against a departmental excavation report. No excavation report, Ancient Ceylon or ASCAR volume was consulted at all, and that is the single largest gap in this block; anything in what_is_disputed about the structure's function should be re-read against the primary archaeological literature before the film is planned.

The coordinates are the Wikipedia point for the site, which matches the OpenStreetMap entry for the ruins and sits inside the citadel area; the temple is separately at about 7.5973, 80.1086 and the museum at about 7.6052, 80.1015, so the circular structure is roughly a few hundred metres south-east of the given point and needs a surveyed position on the ground. The climate note is general district-level material: Kurunegala District covers nine agro-ecological regions of the dry and intermediate zones and drought is common in its northern parts, but no station rainfall series for Hettipola or Wariyapola was obtained, so the recommended months are an informed guess and should be checked against Department of Meteorology data. Drone and filming conditions, including the reported Rs 25,000 per site per week commercial fee and the reported 100-foot altitude ceiling, come from a government filming-permission page and two commercial drone-service pages and are entirely unverified with the Department of Archaeology or the Civil Aviation Authority. Whether the temple community and the site's custodians would welcome a crew has not been asked.

Images: Wikimedia Commons holds thirteen files in the site's category and no more. Five are used here and each was confirmed to exist through action=query&titles= with imageinfo before its URL was written; none is an aerial and none shows the ring's full circle, which is exactly the shot the film exists to get. The file captioned as the circular structure is the uploader's own description, 'Chakravala Kotte ruins', and has not been independently verified as showing that structure.

unknowns: No archaeological excavation report has been read. Everything said here about what the circular structure may have been rests on secondary and tertiary accounts, and the primary literature could overturn several items in what_is_disputed.

Whether the aerial can be flown high enough to close the circle. Registration with the civil aviation authority and clearance from the archaeology department are both required and unverified, and the reported general altitude ceiling is lower than the shot needs.

Whether the inside of the ring can be walked for nearly three hundred metres without touching or destabilising brickwork, and whether the department would permit it. The walking take is the film's spine.
Whether the heat shimmer reads at this scale in the dry months. The treatment depends on it and it has never been tested.
Whether the temple community and the site's custodians would welcome a crew at all, and on what conditions.
The exact surveyed position, extent and present condition of the circular earthwork, and whether the concentric clay rings and the central chamber are legible at ground level today or only in plan.
Whether there is standing water in the moat channel in February and March, which decides whether beat 3 exists as written.
evidence_class_note: Editorial proposal. The location is proposed by Claude from desk research and is unverified; the historical thread is desk research by web search only, with the chronicle read in Geiger's online translation and no archaeological report consulted. No scene or shot is decided here.
